# Heterogeneous Compute Placement\chaptersubtitle{Silicon Interconnects, Memory Bus QoS, and Thermal Envelopes} {#sec-placement}

![**Systems Organ Focus:** Whole-System Heterogeneous Silicon Placement. Partitioning cognitive stages across Cloud Datacenters, Edge Application Processors (MPU), Dedicated Neural Accelerators (NPU), and Microsecond Safety Controllers (MCU) based on computational cadence, memory interconnect bandwidth, and strict hardware fault isolation.](figures/fig_pipeline_locator.svg){#fig-locator-ch10 fig-pos="H" width=100%}

*Why does an autonomous robot that runs flawlessly on the test bench suffer violent latency spikes when deployed inside a sealed chassis?*

In cloud software architecture, computation is treated as an abstract, fungible commodity: microservices are deployed into elastic clusters where physical silicon placement is hidden behind virtualization layers. In Physical AI, silicon topology is a non-negotiable physical boundary. Moving bits across off-chip memory buses consumes orders of magnitude more energy than arithmetic, shared memory crossbars choke when camera DMA bursts contend with neural weight streaming, and unmanaged thermal dissipation triggers hardware downclocking that blows past real-time stopping deadlines. Designing an embodied system requires deliberate workload placement—mapping cognitive stages across cloud servers, Linux host processors, neural accelerators, and real-time microcontrollers based on cadence, memory bandwidth, and physical trust boundaries.

2. **Mitigate Interconnect Contention:** Architect hardware AXI Quality-of-Service (QoS) bus arbitration schemes that guarantee microsecond preemption for real-time safety packets over high-bandwidth video DMA bursts.
3. **Implement Deterministic Shared-Memory IPC:** Construct lock-free, zero-allocation circular ring buffers in tightly coupled SRAM using 64-bit atomic sequence counters and explicit cache maintenance operations.
4. **Quantify the Energy Cost of Data Movement:** Balance arithmetic intensity ($\text{FLOPs/Byte}$) against LPDDR5 DRAM access energy ($150\text{ pJ/access}$) using on-chip SRAM model weight tiling.
5. **Model Dynamic Thermal Dissipation & DVFS:** Derive the junction heating differential equation ($T_j(t)$) and design proactive cadence scaling to prevent thermal downclocking cliffs ($>85^\circ\text{C}$).
6. **Evaluate Re-Placement Ripple Effects:** Quantify how migrating neural models between cloud and edge silicon alters network round-trip jitter, battery endurance, and physical stopping clearance envelopes ($d_{\text{stop}}$).
7. **Dissect Wireless Network Latency Collisions:** Analyze the Insulated Cold-Vault Collision autopsy where a $1,420\text{ ms}$ 5G RF blackout caused a 1.2-ton pallet mover to smash into a structural building pillar at $1.8\text{ m/s}$.

## The Non-Fungibility of Compute in Physical Systems

In modern enterprise software engineering, computation is abstracted behind virtualized infrastructure (@fig-locator-ch10). Developers write containerized services, dispatch tasks to elastic serverless runtimes, and interact with cloud APIs under the assumption that processing power is fungible. If a database query encounters transient congestion or a network packet drops, execution threads block, retry logic absorbs delays, and garbage collectors sweep memory without physical consequence.

In Physical AI Systems, compute is fundamentally **non-fungible** (@fig-heterogeneous-placement). The moment software interacts with physical mass, inertia, and electrical current, the physical location of silicon determines whether the machine survives:

1. **The Physicality of Latency:** Running a 70-billion-parameter Vision-Language Model in a remote cloud datacenter provides immense semantic capacity. However, routing sensor video over a cellular 5G network introduces stochastic Round-Trip Time (RTT) variance ($50\text{--}1500\text{ ms}$) and unannounced RF signal dropouts. If a 1.2-ton mobile machine traveling at $v = 2.0\text{ m/s}$ loses wireless connectivity for one second, the vehicle coasts unguided for two meters ($d_{\text{coast}} = v \cdot \Delta t = 2.0\text{ m}$), turning a wireless packet drop into an unavoidable collision.
2. **The Physics of Memory Energy:** Moving bits across printed circuit board traces consumes orders of magnitude more electrical energy than performing arithmetic operations on those bits. In modern $7\text{ nm}$ silicon, executing an 8-bit integer multiply-accumulate (MAC) operation consumes approximately $0.2\text{ pJ}$, whereas fetching the operand bytes from off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM consumes $150\text{ pJ}$—a $750\times$ energy disparity.
3. **The Thermodynamic Real-Time Cliff:** Compute chips generate thermal energy ($P = I^2 R + C V^2 f$). In a sealed robotic chassis lacking heavy active cooling, sustained neural inference drives silicon junction temperatures past critical thresholds ($T_j > 85^\circ\text{C}$). Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) circuits automatically cut clock frequencies by up to $60\%$, doubling inference latency and causing the robot to miss its hard real-time stopping deadlines.

This physical reality creates sharp tensions among engineering disciplines. Maya, an AI researcher trained in cloud deep learning, naturally seeks to deploy high-capacity 70-billion-parameter foundation models in offboard GPU clusters to maximize open-world semantic generalization. Carlos, an embedded systems engineer, recognizes that unbudgeted wireless latency tails ($> 1\text{ s}$) and on-chip memory bus crossbar contention will starve real-time control loops. Alex, a mechanical and robotics engineer, calculates the inescapable physical consequences: unguided kinetic momentum ($p = mv$) and Joulean package heating ($I^2R$) that can shear mechanical gearboxes or induce thermal shutdown in sealed enclosures.

### The Heterogeneous Silicon Nervous System
To resolve these interdisciplinary tensions, Physical AI organizes silicon into an embodied nervous system that maps cognitive cadence directly to physical hardware substrates:

- **The Strategic Center (Tier 4 - Cloud / Fleet):** Like an offboard library or strategic command room, the cloud aggregates fleet-wide telemetry, performs foundation pre-training, and computes macroscopic routes over minutes or hours ($0.001\text{--}0.1\text{ Hz}$). Separated by high-latency, non-deterministic wide-area networks, it is strictly untrusted for immediate vehicle survival.
- **The Cerebral Cortex (Tier 3 - Linux Host MPU):** Multi-core 64-bit application processors (e.g., ARM Cortex-A78) run full operating systems (Linux with `PREEMPT_RT`), managing rich semantic vision-language models, dynamic coordinate frame trees (`tf2`), and ROS 2 middleware graphs at human cognitive cadences ($0.5\text{--}10\text{ Hz}$). While semantically rich, virtual memory paging, dirty-page flushes, and OS thread scheduling make this tier non-deterministic ($P_{99} > 35\text{ ms}$).
- **The Motor Cortex & Cerebellum (Tier 2 - Neural Accelerator NPU):** Specialized systolic arrays, vector processing units, and edge Tensor Cores execute structured tensor math (such as 1D Temporal U-Nets for Diffusion Policies or ACT decoders) at $20\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$. By operating on multi-step action chunks ($H=16$), this tier generates fluid, reactive motion trajectories while decoupling the fast reflex loops from upstream semantic deliberation.
- **The Spinal Reflex Arc (Tier 1 - Real-Time MCU):** Dedicated 32-bit bare-metal microcontrollers (e.g., ARM Cortex-M7 or lockstep RISC-V) execute in zero-allocation static SRAM (`malloc = 0`) at a deterministic $1000\text{ Hz} \pm 5\,\mu\text{s}$. Holding exclusive hardware access to motor inverter PWM gate drivers, the MCU evaluates Control Barrier Functions, solves minimal-intervention Quadratic Programs, and enforces dynamic stopping envelopes in sub-millisecond real time.

![**The Four-Tier Heterogeneous Compute Topology in Physical AI.** System 2 semantic deliberation maps to Tier 3 Linux MPUs or Tier 4 Cloud clusters; System 1.5 trajectory chunking maps to Tier 2 NPUs; System 1 reflex enforcers map to Tier 1 bare-metal MCUs with direct physical routing to motor inverters.](figures/fig09_heterogeneous_placement.svg){#fig-heterogeneous-placement width=100%}

To satisfy these physical constraints, Physical AI partitions cognitive workloads across a **Four-Tier Heterogeneous Silicon Hierarchy** (@tbl-compute-tiers):

| Compute Fabric Tier | Hardware Substrate | Primary Architectural Role | Typical Execution Cadence | Memory Architecture | Physical Trust Level |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **Tier 4: Cloud / Fleet** | Multi-GPU Datacenter Cluster | Fleet learning, large foundational pre-training, global route planning | $0.001\text{--}0.1\text{ Hz}$ | Terabytes HBM3 / Non-Volatile Storage | **Untrusted:** Non-deterministic WAN latency |
| **Tier 3: Host Processor (MPU)** | 64-bit Multi-Core ARM Cortex-A | Semantic reasoning (VLMs), dynamic frame trees (`tf2`), Linux daemons | $0.5\text{--}10\text{ Hz}$ | 4–16 GB LPDDR5 Unified Memory (UMA) | **Untrusted:** Non-real-time OS jitter ($P_{99} > 100\text{ ms}$) |
| **Tier 2: Neural Accelerator (NPU)** | Systolic Array / Edge Tensor Cores | Spatial affordance tokens (DINOv2), multi-step Action Chunking (ACT, Diffusion) | $20\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$ | On-Chip SRAM Tiling + DRAM DMA | **Untrusted Proposal Service:** High-throughput tensor compute |
| **Tier 1: Real-Time Controller (MCU)** | 32-bit Bare-Metal Cortex-M7 / RISC-V | 1 kHz Control Barrier Functions, dynamic stopping enforcement, PWM motor inverters | **$1000\text{ Hz} \pm 5\,\mu\text{s}$** | 256 KB Zero-Wait-State Internal SRAM | **Fully Trusted Authority:** Sole hardware access to gate drivers |

: Four-Tier Heterogeneous Silicon Placement Hierarchy. Systematic allocation of cognitive organs across compute fabrics based on cadence, memory, and safety privilege. {#tbl-compute-tiers}

This four-tier hierarchy applies across all three canonical Physical AI archetypes. In **Locomotion and Mobility** (such as autonomous transport AGVs and quadrupeds), Tier 4 manages fleet coordination and global warehouse maps ($0.01\text{ Hz}$), Tier 3 processes multi-camera spatial scene graphs ($2\text{ Hz}$), Tier 2 runs receding-horizon diffusion trajectory decoders ($20\text{ Hz}$), and Tier 1 evaluates Control Barrier Functions and commands motor inverters at a deterministic $1000\text{ Hz}$. In **Contact Manipulation** (such as multi-joint robotic arms and dexterous hands), Tier 3 handles semantic task decomposition, Tier 2 executes 50 Hz action-chunked spline policies, and Tier 1 enforces Cartesian contact compliance and joint torque limits in tightly coupled SRAM. In **Cybernetic Process and Energy Regulation** (such as battery energy storage systems and smart inverters), Tier 3 logs degradation trends, Tier 2 runs neural state-of-charge estimators, and Tier 1 bare-metal DSPs execute 20 kHz Space-Vector PWM switching while guarding electrochemical safe sets.

To build an embodied system that thrives within these physical boundaries, this chapter establishes the end-to-end discipline of heterogeneous workload placement. We begin by examining micro-architectural contention across shared on-chip memory crossbars and configuring hardware AXI Quality-of-Service arbitration (Section 10.2). We then construct zero-copy, lock-free SRAM mailboxes that bridge asymmetric Linux host cores and bare-metal microcontrollers without OS scheduling jitter (Section 10.3). Next, we derive the physics of data movement using the Roofline model to balance arithmetic intensity against DRAM access energy (Section 10.4) and model dynamic thermal dissipation to prevent DVFS downclocking cliffs (Section 10.5). We quantify multi-dimensional re-placement ripple effects across latency, power, and safety (Section 10.6), dissect the forensic autopsy of the Insulated Cold-Vault Collision where a 5G wireless blackout caused a 1.2-ton machine to strike a structural pillar (Section 10.7), freeze the formal workload placement specification (**PLACE-01**) that bridges systems architecture to physical integration (Section 10.8), and stress-test the heterogeneous architecture against high-stakes placement dilemmas (Section 10.9).


## Interconnects and Bus Contention

In modern embedded Systems-on-Chip (SoCs)—such as the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, Qualcomm Robotics RB5, or Apple M-series silicon—heterogeneous compute engines (CPU, GPU, NPU, ISP, and DMA engines) share a single pool of physical LPDDR5 DRAM through a **Unified Memory Architecture (UMA)** (@fig-uma-contention).

Unlike desktop workstations where CPUs and discrete GPUs possess separate physical memory pools connected across PCIe expansion buses, an embedded UMA SoC routes all memory traffic through a shared silicon crossbar. While UMA eliminates explicit PCIe data copies, it introduces a severe micro-architectural hazard: **Memory Crossbar Contention**.

![**UMA Memory Bus Contention and AXI QoS Priority Arbitration.** High-bandwidth camera sensor DMA writes ($>1.5\text{ GB/s}$) and NPU model weight fetches ($20\text{ GB/s}$) contend for shared memory crossbars. Without hardware AXI QoS arbitration, unthrottled DMA bursts starve real-time microcontroller reads, causing $1000\text{ Hz}$ safety loops to miss timing deadlines.](figures/fig09_uma_bus_contention.svg){#fig-uma-contention width=100%}

In an unmanaged UMA SoC, multiple bus master engines issue concurrent read/write memory requests across shared AXI interconnect crossbars (such as ARM CoreLink NIC-400 or CCI-550 fabrics):

1. **Camera Sensor DMA Ingestion:** High-resolution multi-camera image sensors write raw uncompressed Bayer frames directly to DRAM via MIPI CSI-2 DMA engines ($1.5\text{--}3.0\text{ GB/s}$ sustained across 4K streams).
2. **NPU Tensor Weight Streaming:** The Neural Processing Unit streams billions of quantized model weights from DRAM into local register files during forward passes ($15\text{--}30\text{ GB/s}$ burst bandwidth).
3. **Real-Time MCU Telemetry Access:** The Real-Time Microcontroller reads joint encoder buffers and writes candidate trajectory waypoints across the shared memory bus.

### Micro-Architectural Head-of-Line Blocking
When an unthrottled camera DMA burst saturates the memory crossbar, DRAM access latency for CPU and MCU cores spikes by $300\text{--}800\%$. The multi-channel memory controller's command queue fills with long-burst transactions (such as 256-byte incrementing bursts, `INCR256`), blocking urgent high-priority requests.

Total memory access latency $t_{\text{access}}$ under bus contention is modeled as:

$$t_{\text{access}} = t_{\text{prop}} + t_{\text{arbitration}} + t_{\text{block}}$$

where $t_{\text{prop}}$ is the baseline silicon propagation delay, $t_{\text{arbitration}}$ is the DRAM row-buffer activation and command arbitration overhead, and $t_{\text{block}}$ represents head-of-line blocking delay:

$$t_{\text{block}} = \frac{N_{\text{burst}} \cdot L_{\text{burst}}}{W_{\text{bus}} \cdot f_{\text{bus}}}$$

where:

- $N_{\text{burst}}$ is the number of pending lower-priority burst transactions queued in the memory controller [dimensionless count].
- $L_{\text{burst}}$ is the burst length per transaction [$\text{Bytes}$] (e.g., $256\text{ bytes}$ for an AXI `INCR256` transaction).
- $W_{\text{bus}}$ is the physical data width of the crossbar interconnect in bytes per clock cycle [$\text{Bytes/cycle}$] (e.g., $16\text{ bytes}$ for a 128-bit crossbar).
- $f_{\text{bus}}$ is the interconnect clock frequency [$\text{Hz}$ or $\text{cycles/s}$] (e.g., $800\text{ MHz}$).

**Concrete Numerical Hazard:** Consider an unmanaged memory crossbar where an unthrottled 4K camera DMA write stream queues $N_{\text{burst}} = 16$ pending $256\text{-byte}$ bursts across a 128-bit ($W_{\text{bus}} = 16\text{ bytes}$) interconnect running at $f_{\text{bus}} = 800\text{ MHz}$. The bus transfer blocking time evaluates to:

$$t_{\text{block}} = \frac{16 \times 256\text{ bytes}}{16\text{ bytes/cycle} \times 800 \times 10^6\text{ cycles/s}} = \frac{4{,}096\text{ bytes}}{12.8 \times 10^9\text{ bytes/s}} = 320\text{ ns}$$

Factoring in DRAM bank conflict and row-activation delay ($t_{\text{arbitration}} \approx 530\text{ ns}$), single-transaction access latency spikes to $t_{\text{access}} \approx 850\text{ ns}$. For a $1000\text{ Hz}$ control loop requiring 20 distinct encoder and waypoint memory reads per millisecond tick, aggregate bus blocking accumulates over:

$$\Delta t_{\text{contention}} = 20 \times 850\text{ ns} = 17.0\,\mu\text{s}$$

In a hard real-time safety Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) with a certified worst-case budget of $\text{WCET} \le 175\,\mu\text{s}$, this $17.0\,\mu\text{s}$ blocking delay consumes nearly $10\%$ of the entire execution window solely waiting on memory crossbar stalls.

### Hardware AXI QoS Priority Arbitration
To eliminate memory crossbar starvation, Physical AI architectures configure hardware **AXI Quality-of-Service (QoS)** arbitration registers (`ARQOS` read and `AWQOS` write 4-bit signals) at the silicon interconnect fabric:

$$\text{AXI QoS Priority Invariant:} \quad \text{QoS}(\text{MCU Real-Time Reads}) > \text{QoS}(\text{NPU Weight Fetches}) > \text{QoS}(\text{Camera DMA Writes})$$

1. **Real-Time MCU SRAM/DRAM Reads (`QoS = 15`):** Absolute highest interconnect priority (value `0b1111`). AXI crossbar arbiters immediately preempt lower-priority transactions at the next 64-bit beat boundary ($1.25\text{ ns}$) and insert MCU read requests at the head of the DRAM controller scheduler queue, guaranteeing transaction service within $<45\text{ ns}$ and total loop memory delay $<0.90\,\mu\text{s}$.
2. **NPU Tensor Weight Fetches (`QoS = 10`):** Medium-high priority (value `0b1010`), guaranteeing sustained memory throughput ($15\text{--}30\text{ GB/s}$) to meet $20\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$ action chunking deadlines without starving the real-time controller.
3. **Camera Sensor DMA Writes (`QoS = 4`):** Background priority (value `0b0100`). Camera DMA streams are buffered in dedicated on-chip hardware FIFO buffers and paced onto the crossbar using token-bucket rate limiters only during memory bus idle cycles, completely eliminating latency tail blowouts for critical safety loops.

::: {.callout-fallacy title="Wireless Offloading for Real-Time Reflexes"}
* **The Common Assumption:** High-speed 5G URLLC and Wi-Fi 7 networks offer sub-$5\text{ ms}$ nominal round-trip times and multi-gigabit throughput, making it feasible to offload high-frequency motor reflex loops and safety controllers to edge cloud GPU servers to save onboard battery power and compute weight.
* **The Physical Reality:** Wireless radio frequency (RF) propagation is inherently stochastic. Moving steel machinery, reinforced concrete walls, and insulated panels create RF multipath fading nulls and Faraday shadow blackouts where tail latency spikes beyond $1400\text{ ms}$ ($P(\text{blackout} > 1.0\text{ s}) > 0$). If a 1.2-ton machine moving at $v = 1.8\text{ m/s}$ offloads reflex authority to an edge server, an unexpected $1.4\text{ s}$ network drop results in $2.55\text{ m}$ of unguided kinetic travel, causing catastrophic impact collisions.
* **The Systems Invariant:** Real-time reflexes ($1000\text{ Hz}$) and dynamic stopping enforcement must execute locally on bare-metal microcontroller silicon physically wired to actuator gate drivers. Wireless offloading is restricted strictly to macroscopic deliberation and global intent generation governed by Expiring Intent Leases ($\Delta t_{\text{lease}} \le 300\text{ ms}$).
:::


## Lock-Free Shared SRAM Mailboxes

To pass high-rate trajectory chunks ($50\text{ Hz}$) and low-latency safety telemetry ($1000\text{ Hz}$) between the Linux host MPU and the bare-metal MCU without thread blocking, Physical AI rejects traditional operating system IPC primitives (such as Unix domain sockets, POSIX message queues, or kernel mutexes). 

Under Linux, acquiring a contested mutex involves kernel `futex` system calls, CPU thread context switches, and core migrations that routinely introduce $10\text{--}50\text{ ms}$ of non-deterministic scheduling jitter. Crucially, a bare-metal microcontroller executing in zero-allocation static SRAM has no operating system kernel, cannot block on user-space semaphores, and cannot interact with Linux scheduler runqueues.

Instead, inter-processor communication is implemented using **Zero-Copy Lock-Free Single-Producer Single-Consumer (SPSC) Ring Buffers** residing in physical internal static SRAM (Tightly Coupled Memory - TCM).

### Memory Ordering, False Sharing, and Cache Maintenance
Operating across asymmetric silicon domains (e.g., an out-of-order 64-bit ARM Cortex-A78 running Linux and a deterministic 32-bit ARM Cortex-M7 running bare-metal) requires strict memory isolation:

1. **Cache Line Alignment and False Sharing:** Modern CPU cores manage memory in 64-byte cache lines. If producer and consumer control variables reside within the same 64-byte window, the hardware cache coherency interconnect continuously bounces the line between cores (cache line ping-pong via MESI snooping), degrading throughput by over $10\times$. All mailbox control structures and payload slots are strictly isolated using 64-byte alignment (`alignas(64)`).
2. **Atomic Monotonic Sequence Counters:** The producer increments `head_sequence` using 64-bit atomic operations with release memory barriers (`atomic_store_explicit(&mailbox->head_sequence, seq, memory_order_release)` or ARM `dmb ish`). The consumer reads the sequence using acquire memory barriers (`atomic_load_explicit(&mailbox->head_sequence, memory_order_acquire)` or ARM `dmb ish`), guaranteeing that payload data writes are fully committed across the memory fabric before the sequence counter updates.
3. **Explicit Cache Line Invalidation to Point of Coherency (PoC):** Because the Cortex-A processor operates with hierarchical L1/L2 data caches while the Cortex-M microcontroller accesses tightly coupled SRAM without hardware cache snooping, software must explicitly maintain cache coherency:

$$\text{Producer Write Sequence:} \quad \text{write\_payload}(\text{slot}) \implies \text{clean\_dcache\_range}(\text{addr}, \text{size}) \implies \text{atomic\_store}(\text{head})$$

$$\text{Consumer Read Sequence:} \quad \text{atomic\_load}(\text{head}) \implies \text{invalidate\_dcache\_range}(\text{addr}, \text{size}) \implies \text{read\_payload}(\text{slot})$$

### Latest-Frame Sampling Semantics
The lock-free SPSC ring buffer naturally bridges the cadence mismatch between multi-rate cognitive organs. When Maya's 50 Hz trajectory planner publishes 16-waypoint action chunks faster than Carlos's 1000 Hz MCU reflex loop consumes entire batches, the consumer does not process an unbounded FIFO queue. Instead, it executes **Latest-Frame Sampling**:

$$\text{slot\_idx} = \text{head\_sequence} \pmod{N_{\text{slots}}}$$

$$\tau_{\text{staleness}} = t_{\text{sample}} - t_{\text{publish}} \le \frac{1}{f_{\text{producer}}} = T_{\text{chunk}}$$

where:

- $\text{slot\_idx}$ is the physical buffer index into the triple-buffered SRAM mailbox [dimensionless integer $\in \{0, 1, 2\}$].
- $\text{head\_sequence}$ is the monotonically increasing 64-bit atomic transaction counter [count].
- $N_{\text{slots}} = 3$ is the triple-buffered slot allocation preventing writer-reader memory collisions.
- $\tau_{\text{staleness}}$ is the maximum age of the ingested trajectory data [$\text{seconds}$].
- $f_{\text{producer}}$ is the publishing cadence of the neural trajectory planner [$\text{Hz}$] ($50\text{ Hz} \implies T_{\text{chunk}} = 20.0\text{ ms}$).

**Concrete Operational Mechanics:** If the producer publishes at $f_{\text{producer}} = 50\text{ Hz}$ ($T_{\text{chunk}} = 20.0\text{ ms}$) into a 3-slot ring buffer, and the consumer samples at $f_{\text{consumer}} = 1000\text{ Hz}$ ($T_{\text{cycle}} = 1.0\text{ ms}$), the latest-frame sampling mechanism drops intermediate stale waypoints without memory allocation or blocking. It guarantees that the sampled trajectory chunk is never older than $20.0\text{ ms}$, feeding smooth quintic spline interpolators on the microcontroller with zero queue lag.

```c
// Lock-Free Shared SRAM Trajectory Mailbox (SPSC)
// Target: Asymmetric Cortex-A78 (Linux) <-> Cortex-M7 (Bare-Metal SRAM)
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdatomic.h>
#include <stdalign.h>

#define SRAM_BUFFER_SLOTS 3
#define WAYPOINT_CHUNK_SIZE 16

typedef struct {
    float pos[3];       // Cartesian Position [m]
    float vel[3];       // Cartesian Velocity [m/s]
    float acc[3];       // Cartesian Acceleration [m/s^2]
    uint32_t timestamp_us;
} Waypoint_t;

typedef struct alignas(64) {
    Waypoint_t waypoints[WAYPOINT_CHUNK_SIZE];
    uint32_t chunk_id;
    uint32_t crc32;
    uint8_t padding[64 - ((sizeof(Waypoint_t)*WAYPOINT_CHUNK_SIZE + 8) % 64)];
} TrajectorySlot_t;

typedef struct alignas(64) {
    // Producer control (Linux Host MPU)
    alignas(64) _Atomic uint64_t head_sequence;
    
    // Consumer control (Bare-Metal MCU)
    alignas(64) _Atomic uint64_t tail_sequence;
    
    // Triple-buffered payload slots in internal static SRAM
    alignas(64) TrajectorySlot_t slots[SRAM_BUFFER_SLOTS];
} SPSCSharedMailbox_t;

// Producer (Linux MPU 50 Hz): Zero-Allocation Write
void mailbox_publish(SPSCSharedMailbox_t *mb, const TrajectorySlot_t *new_chunk) {
    uint64_t seq = atomic_load_explicit(&mb->head_sequence, memory_order_relaxed);
    uint32_t slot_idx = (seq + 1) % SRAM_BUFFER_SLOTS;
    
    // 1. Copy payload into target SRAM slot
    mb->slots[slot_idx] = *new_chunk;
    
    // 2. Explicit cache clean to Point of Coherency (PoC) for non-coherent domain
    clean_dcache_range((uintptr_t)&mb->slots[slot_idx], sizeof(TrajectorySlot_t));
    
    // 3. Atomic store with release memory barrier (dmb ish)
    atomic_store_explicit(&mb->head_sequence, seq + 1, memory_order_release);
}

// Consumer (MCU 1000 Hz): Lock-Free Latest-Frame Ingestion
int mailbox_sample_latest(SPSCSharedMailbox_t *mb, TrajectorySlot_t *out_chunk) {
    // 1. Atomic load with acquire memory barrier
    uint64_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&mb->head_sequence, memory_order_acquire);
    uint64_t tail = atomic_load_explicit(&mb->tail_sequence, memory_order_relaxed);
    
    if (head == tail) {
        return 0; // No new trajectory chunk published
    }
    
    uint32_t latest_slot = head % SRAM_BUFFER_SLOTS;
    
    // 2. Invalidate cache line before reading shared SRAM
    invalidate_dcache_range((uintptr_t)&mb->slots[latest_slot], sizeof(TrajectorySlot_t));
    
    // 3. Read payload and update consumed tail counter
    *out_chunk = mb->slots[latest_slot];
    atomic_store_explicit(&mb->tail_sequence, head, memory_order_release);
    return 1; // Fresh chunk successfully acquired (staleness <= 20 ms)
}
```

::: {.callout-fallacy title="Zero-Copy Shared SRAM Mailboxes Without Hardware Memory Barriers"}
* **The Common Assumption:** Passing pointers to statically allocated shared SRAM structures between asymmetric CPU and MCU cores allows zero-copy inter-processor communication without any synchronization overhead or execution delay.
* **The Physical Reality:** Modern out-of-order application processors (e.g., ARM Cortex-A78) and multi-channel interconnects aggressively reorder memory store instructions to maximize throughput. Without explicit hardware Data Memory Barriers (`__DMB()`, `dmb ish`) and cache maintenance operations (`clean_dcache_range`), the producer core may update the atomic `head_sequence` index in DRAM before the actual waypoint payload bytes are committed across the memory crossbar. The real-time microcontroller reads uncommitted or partially written memory slots (torn reads), interpolating corrupted trajectory data that drives joints into violent high-frequency torque chatter.
* **The Systems Invariant:** Shared-memory IPC across asymmetric silicon domains must enforce strict cache line isolation (`alignas(64)`), acquire-release atomic ordering, and hardware cache clean/invalidate operations to the Point of Coherency (PoC) before sequence counters are published.
:::


## Arithmetic Intensity and the Roofline Model

In physical systems design, the total electrical power budget is constrained by onboard battery capacity and thermal dissipation limits. To maximize operational battery life and prevent thermal runaway, algorithms must be optimized for **Arithmetic Intensity** ($I_{\text{arith}}$), defined as the ratio of computational floating-point operations to memory access traffic [@hennessy2019computer; @williams2009roofline]:

$$I_{\text{arith}} = \frac{\Phi_{\text{FLOPs}}}{\text{BW}_{\text{DRAM}}} = \frac{\text{Total Operations (FLOPs)}}{\text{Total Memory Traffic (Bytes)}} \quad \left[ \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Byte}} \right]$$

The hardware Roofline model dictates whether a neural policy is bound by computational throughput or memory bus bandwidth:

$$\text{Attainable Performance (FLOPs/s)} = \min\left( \pi_{\text{peak}}, \; I_{\text{arith}} \times \beta_{\text{mem}} \right)$$

The transition between operational regimes is defined by the hardware **Ridge Point** ($\beta_{\text{ridge}}$):

$$\beta_{\text{ridge}} = \frac{\pi_{\text{peak}}}{\beta_{\text{mem}}} \quad \left[ \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Byte}} \right]$$

where:

- $\pi_{\text{peak}}$ is the peak theoretical compute throughput of the accelerator [$\text{FLOPs/s}$].
- $\beta_{\text{mem}}$ is the peak sustained memory bus bandwidth [$\text{Bytes/s}$].
- $\beta_{\text{ridge}}$ is the hardware ridge point separating memory-bound from compute-bound regimes [$\text{FLOPs/Byte}$].
- $\Phi_{\text{FLOPs}}$ is the operational floating-point execution rate [$\text{FLOPs/s}$].
- $\text{BW}_{\text{DRAM}}$ is the off-chip DRAM memory bus bandwidth [$\text{Bytes/s}$].

### Memory-Bound vs. Compute-Bound Regimes
The hardware Roofline curve divides all neural workloads into two operational regimes:

1. **Memory-Bandwidth Bound ($I_{\text{arith}} < \beta_{\text{ridge}}$):** Computational throughput is strictly limited by the rate at which bytes can be fetched across off-chip memory traces. The accelerator's tensor ALUs spend $>90\%$ of their clock cycles stalled waiting for DRAM operands, while memory bus PHY I/O pads dissipate substantial electrical power.
2. **Compute Bound ($I_{\text{arith}} \ge \beta_{\text{ridge}}$):** Tensor ALUs operate at peak saturation. Memory bus transfer times are completely hidden behind arithmetic execution pipelines.

Total electrical power dissipated by compute and memory silicon is governed by:

$$P_{\text{total}} = P_{\text{ALU}} + P_{\text{DRAM\_IO}} = (\Phi_{\text{FLOPs}} \times E_{\text{op}}) + (\text{BW}_{\text{DRAM}} \times E_{\text{DRAM\_byte}})$$

where $E_{\text{op}}$ is the energy consumed per arithmetic operation [$\text{Joules/FLOP}$] ($\approx 0.2\text{ pJ}$ for an INT8 multiply-accumulate operation in modern $7\text{ nm}$ silicon), and $E_{\text{DRAM\_byte}}$ is the physical I/O pad and DRAM bank access energy per transferred byte [$\text{Joules/Byte}$] ($\approx 150\text{ pJ/Byte}$ in LPDDR5 DRAM).

### Side-by-Side Architectural Evaluation
Consider a concrete numerical comparison between two deployment architectures on an autonomous mobile platform:

* **Architecture A: Unquantized Single-Token VLA on DRAM:** An unquantized 7-billion-parameter model executing autoregressively fetches $7.0\text{ GB}$ of FP16 model weights per action token. Generating 10 tokens per second ($10\text{ Hz}$) demands $70.0\text{ GB/s}$ of continuous DRAM memory bandwidth ($\text{BW}_{\text{DRAM}} = 70.0 \times 10^9\text{ Bytes/s}$). At $E_{\text{DRAM\_byte}} \approx 150\text{ pJ/byte}$, the memory I/O interface alone dissipates:
  $$P_{\text{DRAM\_IO}} = 70.0 \times 10^9\text{ Bytes/s} \times 150 \times 10^{-12}\text{ J/Byte} = 10.50\text{ Watts}$$
  Because single-token generation executes approximately $14.0\text{ GFLOPs/token}$ ($14.0 \times 10^9\text{ FLOPs/s}$), the operational arithmetic intensity is:
  $$I_{\text{arith}} = \frac{14.0 \times 10^9\text{ FLOPs/s}}{70.0 \times 10^9\text{ Bytes/s}} = 0.20\text{ FLOPs/Byte} \ll \beta_{\text{ridge}} \approx 120\text{ FLOPs/Byte}$$
  This $10.50\text{ W}$ memory bus power draw occurs entirely in PHY I/O pads and DRAM banks before arithmetic is performed, trapping the processor in the memory-bound regime where ALUs are stalled $>95\%$ of the time.

* **Architecture B: Quantized Action-Chunked Policy in On-Chip SRAM:** An INT8-quantized 1D Temporal U-Net diffusion policy ($6.5\text{ MB}$ total parameter footprint) resides permanently inside the neural accelerator's $8\text{ MB}$ on-chip static SRAM. Generating a 16-step action chunk requires $1.2\text{ GFLOPs}$ of computation ($60.0\text{ GFLOPs/s}$ at $50\text{ Hz}$) while generating zero off-chip DRAM traffic ($\text{BW}_{\text{DRAM}} = 0\text{ GB/s}$). At internal SRAM access energy $E_{\text{SRAM}} \approx 1.5\text{ pJ/byte}$, total data movement power is:
  $$P_{\text{SRAM\_IO}} = 50\text{ Hz} \times 6.5 \times 10^6\text{ Bytes} \times 1.5 \times 10^{-12}\text{ J/Byte} = 0.00049\text{ Watts} = 0.49\text{ mW}$$
  Operational arithmetic intensity surges to $I_{\text{arith}} > 180\text{ FLOPs/Byte} > \beta_{\text{ridge}}$, operating squarely in the compute-bound regime, slashing data movement heat by $99.9\%$, and enabling sustained $50\text{ Hz}$ inference within a compact $8\text{ W}$ total SoC power envelope.

To achieve maximum computational efficiency, Physical AI architectures apply three silicon optimizations:

1. **On-Chip SRAM Weight Tiling:** High-frequency trajectory decoders (such as 1D Temporal U-Nets for Diffusion Policies in Contact Manipulation) are quantized to INT8 or FP8 precision, enabling the entire active model weights ($<8\text{ MB}$) to reside permanently inside the NPU's on-chip static SRAM.
2. **Elimination of Off-Chip DRAM Round-Trips:** By keeping model weights and intermediate activations in on-chip SRAM across layers, memory bus traffic is reduced to zero during trajectory generation, increasing arithmetic intensity to $I_{\text{arith}} > 150\text{ FLOPs/Byte}$.
3. **Joulean Energy Savings:** Operating out of SRAM ($E_{\text{SRAM}} \approx 1.5\text{ pJ}$) cuts data movement energy by $98.5\%$, allowing the neural accelerator to sustain $50\text{ Hz}$ action chunking while drawing under $12\text{ Watts}$ of total package power.

::: {.callout-fallacy title="Arithmetic Intensity Neglect in Embedded Model Sizing"}
* **The Common Assumption:** Sizing a foundation model for embedded robotics based solely on total parameter count ($N$) and theoretical FLOP throughput ensures the model will execute within the edge compute budget.
* **The Physical Reality:** Computational throughput (FLOPs/s) is useless if the workload is trapped in the memory-bandwidth-bound regime of the Roofline curve ($I_{\text{arith}} < \beta_{\text{ridge}}$). Single-batch autoregressive token generation fetches multi-gigabyte weight tensors across DRAM for every individual step ($I_{\text{arith}} \approx 1.0\text{ FLOPs/Byte}$). At $150\text{ pJ/Byte}$ DRAM access energy, memory PHY I/O pads dissipate $10.5\text{ W}$ of heat purely shuffling weights, driving silicon junction temperature past $85^\circ\text{C}$ and triggering hardware DVFS downclocking that halves inference throughput.
* **The Systems Invariant:** Trajectory generation policies deployed on power-constrained edge SoCs must be designed for the compute-bound Roofline regime ($I_{\text{arith}} \ge 120\text{ FLOPs/Byte}$), leveraging temporal action chunking ($H \ge 16$) and model parameter footprints small enough ($<8\text{ MB}$) to tile permanently in on-chip static SRAM.
:::


## Thermal Envelopes and Dynamic Throttling

All electrical energy consumed by silicon computing substrates is ultimately converted into thermal heat via Joule heating ($P = I^2 R$). In an embodied robot, compute silicon is frequently housed inside a sealed, IP67-rated water-resistant chassis lacking heavy active cooling fans (@fig-thermal-derating).

![**Thermodynamic Junction Heating and the DVFS Downclocking Cliff.** Sustained high-load neural inference dissipates thermal heat. When junction temperature breaches $T_j > 85^\circ\text{C}$, hardware DVFS circuits downclock the accelerator by up to $60\%$, doubling inference latency and causing the robot to miss its real-time stopping deadlines. Proactive cadence scaling manages thermal equilibrium.](figures/fig09_thermal_derating_ripple.svg){#fig-thermal-derating width=100%}

The thermodynamic heat dissipation of the compute die is governed by the lumped-parameter thermal RC differential equation:

$$C_{\text{th}} \frac{d T_j(t)}{dt} = P_{\text{dynamic}}(t) + P_{\text{leakage}}(T_j) - \frac{T_j(t) - T_{\text{ambient}}}{R_{\text{th}}}$$

where:

- $T_j(t)$ is the instantaneous silicon junction temperature [$^\circ\text{C}$].
- $T_{\text{ambient}}$ is the ambient enclosure temperature [$^\circ\text{C}$].
- $C_{\text{th}}$ is the lumped thermal capacitance of the silicon die and copper heat spreader [$\text{Joules}/^\circ\text{C}$ or $\text{J/K}$].
- $R_{\text{th}}$ is the thermal resistance from junction to ambient air through the aluminum chassis [$\text{K}/\text{W}$].
- $\tau_{\text{th}} = R_{\text{th}} C_{\text{th}}$ represents the thermal time constant of the silicon package [$\text{seconds}$].
- $P_{\text{dynamic}} = \alpha C V^2 f$ is the dynamic switching power dissipated by active transistor gates [$\text{Watts}$].
- $P_{\text{leakage}}(T_j) \propto T_j^2 e^{-q V_{\text{th}} / k T_j}$ is static sub-threshold leakage power that grows exponentially with junction temperature [$\text{Watts}$].

Under sustained neural inference workload $P_{\text{total}} = P_{\text{dynamic}} + P_{\text{leakage}}$, the transient thermal step response starting from ambient equilibrium $T_j(0) = T_{\text{ambient}}$ is:

$$T_j(t) = T_{\text{ambient}} + P_{\text{total}} R_{\text{th}} \left( 1 - e^{-t / \tau_{\text{th}}} \right)$$

The asymptotic steady-state equilibrium junction temperature reaches:

$$T_{\text{ss}} = T_{\text{ambient}} + P_{\text{total}} R_{\text{th}}$$

The elapsed operating time $t_{\text{trip}}$ required to reach a critical thermal shutdown or throttling threshold $T_{\text{trip}}$ is:

$$t_{\text{trip}} = -\tau_{\text{th}} \ln\left( 1 - \frac{T_{\text{trip}} - T_{\text{ambient}}}{P_{\text{total}} R_{\text{th}}} \right)$$

### Concrete Numerical Evaluation
Consider an autonomous mobile robot with an onboard compute module enclosed in an IP67 sealed aluminum chassis ($T_{\text{ambient}} = 45.0^\circ\text{C}$ on a warm factory floor). The compute package exhibits a thermal resistance of $R_{\text{th}} = 1.80\text{ K/W}$ and a thermal capacitance of $C_{\text{th}} = 25.0\text{ J/K}$, yielding a thermal time constant of $\tau_{\text{th}} = R_{\text{th}} C_{\text{th}} = 45.0\text{ seconds}$.

* **Unmanaged High-Load Inference ($P_{\text{total}} = 25.0\text{ W}$):** Under continuous, unthrottled neural inference, the equilibrium steady-state junction temperature evaluates to:
  $$T_{\text{ss}} = 45.0^\circ\text{C} + (25.0\text{ W} \times 1.80\text{ K/W}) = 45.0 + 45.0 = 90.0^\circ\text{C}$$
  Because $T_{\text{ss}} = 90.0^\circ\text{C} > 85.0^\circ\text{C}$, the silicon will breach the critical safety threshold ($T_{\text{trip}} = 85.0^\circ\text{C}$). The time elapsed before throttling trips is:
  $$t_{\text{trip}} = -45.0 \ln\left(1 - \frac{85.0 - 45.0}{25.0 \times 1.80}\right) = -45.0 \ln\left(1 - \frac{40.0}{45.0}\right) = -45.0 \ln\left(\frac{1}{9}\right) = 45.0 \ln(9) \approx 98.88\text{ s} \approx 98.9\text{ s}$$
  At $t = 98.9\text{ seconds}$, the hardware DVFS downclocking cliff triggers, forcing clock frequencies down by $60\%$ and halving inference throughput mid-mission.

* **Proactive Cadence Scaling ($P_{\text{total}} \to 12.0\text{ W}$):** When firmware detects $T_j \ge 75.0^\circ\text{C}$ and proactively expands the chunk horizon ($H=16 \to 32$) while scaling cadence ($50\text{ Hz} \to 20\text{ Hz}$), total power drops to $12.0\text{ W}$. The new equilibrium stabilizes at:
  $$T_{\text{ss}} = 45.0^\circ\text{C} + (12.0\text{ W} \times 1.80\text{ K/W}) = 45.0 + 21.6 = 66.6^\circ\text{C}$$
  This safely caps package heating well below $80.0^\circ\text{C}$, completely preventing DVFS clock throttling while preserving real-time control deadlines.

### The DVFS Downclocking Cliff
Compute SoCs implement hardware **Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS)** thermal trip points:

1. **Nominal Operating Regime ($T_j \le 75^\circ\text{C}$):** The accelerator operates at maximum rated boost clock frequency ($f_{\text{boost}} = 1.3\text{ GHz}$), sustaining $50\text{ Hz}$ diffusion policy inference ($T_{\text{infer}} = 18.0\text{ ms}$).
2. **Thermal Trip Threshold ($T_j \ge 85^\circ\text{C}$):** To prevent permanent semiconductor lattice degradation, the SoC's hardware Power Management IC (PMIC) triggers thermal throttling, forcing the clock frequency down by $60\%$ ($f_{\text{throttle}} = 520\text{ MHz}$).
3. **The Real-Time Deadline Violation:** Downclocking causes diffusion inference latency to jump from $18.0\text{ ms}$ to $45.0\text{ ms}$. If the System 1.5 trajectory planner requires a new action chunk every $20.0\text{ ms}$ ($50\text{ Hz}$), the throttled accelerator drops half its execution frames, starving the $1000\text{ Hz}$ real-time trajectory queue. Moving mass coasts unguided through missing spline segments, triggering emergency safety stops.

To avoid the DVFS downclocking cliff, Physical AI systems implement **Proactive Thermal Cadence Scaling**:

$$T_j \ge 75^\circ\text{C} \implies \text{Reduce Cadence from } 50\text{ Hz } (H=16) \longrightarrow 20\text{ Hz } (H=32)$$

By doubling the action chunk horizon from $H=16$ to $H=32$, the policy halves its forward inference rate ($50\text{ Hz} \to 20\text{ Hz}$), cutting dynamic switching power ($P_{\text{dynamic}}$) by $60\%$. Silicon junction temperature stabilizes below $78^\circ\text{C}$, maintaining continuous, deterministic real-time control without tripping hardware thermal downclocking.

::: {.callout-fallacy title="Steady-State Thermal Benchmarking in Ambient Free Air"}
* **The Common Assumption:** Benchmarking an edge compute SoC on an open laboratory bench at $22^\circ\text{C}$ ambient temperature proves that a 25 W neural workload is thermally viable for production robotics.
* **The Physical Reality:** Silicon thermal dynamics follow a first-order differential response governed by thermal resistance $R_{\text{th}}$ and thermal capacitance $C_{\text{th}}$ ($\tau_{\text{th}} = R_{\text{th}} C_{\text{th}} \approx 45\text{ s}$). Short bench tests evaluate only the transient thermal capacitance phase, failing to reach steady-state junction equilibrium ($T_{\text{ss}} = T_{\text{ambient}} + P_{\text{total}} R_{\text{th}}$). In an IP67-sealed chassis operating in a $45^\circ\text{C}$ ambient warehouse, sustained inference at $P_{\text{total}} = 25\text{ W}$ drives $T_{\text{ss}}$ to $90^\circ\text{C}$, triggering hardware DVFS downclocking at $t \approx 99\text{ s}$. The sudden $60\%$ drop in clock frequency doubles inference latency and starves control loops mid-operation.
* **The Systems Invariant:** Embedded thermal envelopes must be validated under continuous worst-case steady-state equilibrium ($t \ge 5\tau_{\text{th}}$). Firmware must implement Proactive Thermal Cadence Scaling ($T_j \ge 75^\circ\text{C} \implies 50\text{ Hz} \to 20\text{ Hz}$) to stabilize junction temperatures below the DVFS downclocking cliff.
:::


## Workload Re-Placement Cascades

When designing a Physical AI system, architects frequently consider re-partitioning algorithms across compute fabrics (e.g., migrating a Vision-Language Model from an offboard cloud cluster to an onboard edge NPU, or shifting state estimation from an MCU to a Linux thread). 

Every re-placement decision triggers a multi-dimensional ripple effect across latency, power, thermal headroom, and safety (@tbl-placement-tradeoffs):

| Architectural Re-Placement Choice | Primary Advantage | Silicon Latency Impact | Thermal & Power Impact | Safety & Robustness Consequence |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Offload System 2 VLA to Cloud / 5G** | Unlocks massive 70B parameter models; saves onboard battery | Adds $50\text{--}1500\text{ ms}$ WAN jitter; subject to RF drops | Reduces onboard compute power by $\sim 30\text{ W}$ | **Vulnerable:** Must enforce hard local MCU fallback leases |
| **Quantize VLA to 3B on Edge NPU** | Fully autonomous offline operation; zero RF network dependence | Deterministic $350\text{ ms}$ local inference latency | Increases onboard TDP by $25\text{ W}$; raises $T_j$ | **Robust:** Immune to wireless dropouts and jamming |
| **Move State Estimation from MCU to Linux MPU** | Access to rich ROS2 / Python sensor fusion libraries | Injects $5\text{--}50\text{ ms}$ OS scheduling jitter | Negligible power delta ($<1\text{ W}$) | **Dangerous:** OS page faults freeze state belief during motion |
| **Move Reflex CBF-QP from Linux to Bare-Metal MCU** | Deterministic sub-millisecond execution ($\text{WCET} \le 175\,\mu\text{s}$) | Reduces safety response latency from $50\text{ ms} \to 1.0\text{ ms}$ | Negligible power footprint ($<0.5\text{ W}$) | **Provably Safe:** Hardware-isolated from OS stalls and crashes |

: Architectural Re-Placement Ripple Effects. Trade-offs across computational capability, latency determinism, thermal dissipation, and physical safety. {#tbl-placement-tradeoffs}

Analyzing these ripple effects illuminates why physical placement cannot be decoupled from mechanical dynamics:

1. **Cloud Offload Trade-offs:** Maya's desire to offload 70B VLM deliberation to the cloud frees $30\text{ W}$ of onboard electrical power and extends battery runtime. However, Alex notes that unbuffered 5G latency tails turn wireless packet drops into unguided momentum ($p = mv$). Cloud offloading is only admissible if high-level commands are encapsulated within time-bounded **Expiring Intent Leases** ($\tau_{\text{lease}} \le 100\text{ ms}$), allowing local microcontrollers to safely decelerate if network communication stalls.
2. **Edge NPU Quantization:** Quantizing foundation models into 3B parameter edge variants eliminates external RF dependencies, ensuring complete operational autonomy in RF-shielded environments. However, Carlos and Alex must co-design the physical chassis to dissipate the additional $25\text{ W}$ of continuous thermal dissipation without triggering DVFS downclocking.
3. **The State Estimation Trap:** Shifting state estimation (such as Kalman filtering or Lie-algebraic pose tracking) from bare-metal microcontrollers to Linux host user-space allows developers to use extensive open-source robotics libraries. However, non-deterministic Linux kernel page faults and thread migrations inject $5\text{--}50\text{ ms}$ of scheduling jitter into the state belief, corrupting numerical velocity derivatives ($\dot{\mathbf{x}} \approx \frac{\Delta \mathbf{x}}{\Delta t}$) and destabilizing high-speed feedback controllers.
4. **The Bare-Metal Reflex Invariant:** Migrating Control Barrier Function Quadratic Programs (CBF-QPs) from Linux to a bare-metal microcontroller reduces safety response latency from $50\text{ ms}$ down to a deterministic $\text{WCET} \le 175\,\mu\text{s}$, mathematically guaranteeing that safety invariants are enforced even during complete host operating system kernel panics.

The cardinal rule of Physical AI placement dictates: **Never migrate time-critical safety authority across an asynchronous or non-deterministic boundary**. Semantic deliberation may be offloaded to cloud servers if protected by local intent leases, but real-time state estimation and reflex barrier enforcement must remain permanently anchored to local, bare-metal silicon.

::: {.callout-fallacy title="Local Dynamic Re-Placement Cascades and Hidden Bus Contention"}
* **The Common Assumption:** If an onboard compute fabric runs out of capacity, dynamically migrating an algorithm (such as point cloud filtering or state estimation) to another onboard core (e.g., from MCU to host Linux MPU) resolves the bottleneck with minimal ripple effect.
* **The Physical Reality:** Re-placing a workload alters memory traffic patterns across the entire shared SoC crossbar. Moving high-rate sensor processing from an isolated SRAM MCU to Linux user-space forces multi-megabyte image and point cloud buffers to traverse the shared LPDDR5 DRAM bus. The resulting bus contention delays NPU weight fetches and inflates camera DMA latency, causing cascading deadline misses in downstream trajectory decoders.
* **The Systems Invariant:** Workload placement across heterogeneous silicon must be statically budgeted and verified across all shared contention domains (DRAM bandwidth, AXI interconnect queues, thermal package limits) using fixed engineering ledgers (**PLACE-01**) before runtime deployment.
:::


## Incident Autopsy: Cold-Vault Wireless Blackout

The destructive physical reality of offloading time-critical policy execution across a non-deterministic wireless network is documented in the forensic autopsy of an autonomous heavy transport AGV.

::: {.callout-autopsy title="The Insulated Cold-Vault Collision"}
**Platform:** 1.2-ton Autonomous Heavy Pallet Mover ($m = 1{,}200\text{ kg}$, $v = 1.8\text{ m/s}$).  
**Failure Mechanism:** To reduce onboard compute costs and thermal dissipation, the high-level VLA policy was offloaded to an edge 5G server; entering a cold-storage vault created an RF multipath and shadow blackout of $1,420\text{ ms}$.  
**Root Cause:** Drive torque commands remained latched at $240\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ during the wireless dropout without local fallback trajectory caches or an independent MCU stopping supervisor.  
**Physical Consequence:** The vehicle coasted unguided for $2.556\text{ m}$ ($+1.356\text{ m}$ past physical obstacle clearance), smashing into a structural steel pillar at $1.8\text{ m/s}$ ($E_k = 1{,}944\text{ J}$), shearing the front steering kingpin, rupturing hydraulic lines, and crushing lithium battery modules ($42{,}000\text{ USD}$ overhaul).  
:::

![The Autonomous Heavy Pallet Mover Platform. Offloading policy execution to a 5G edge server caused a fatal crash when entering a cold-storage vault that blocked RF signals for $1,420\text{ ms}$.](figures/fig09_agv_mover_cropped.jpg){#fig-agv-mover width=100%}

In this industrial incident, a 1.2-ton automated guided vehicle (AGV) was transporting heavy palletized goods across a distribution warehouse at an operational velocity of $v = 1.8\text{ m/s}$ ($6.48\text{ km/h}$) (@fig-agv-mover). To minimize onboard thermal dissipation, bill-of-materials cost, and battery consumption, systems architects offloaded the multi-camera vision-language-action (VLA) policy to an offboard edge computing server over a private 5G Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) network.

At timestamp $T + 84.210\text{ s}$, the AGV crossed the doorway threshold into an industrial cold-storage refrigeration vault. The vault walls were constructed of double-sided steel-clad polyurethane insulation panels, forming a continuous Faraday cage. The RF signal-to-noise ratio collapsed immediately from $+24\text{ dB}$ to $0\text{ dB}$, and the 5G connection entered an unannounced $1,420\text{ ms}$ packet blackout.

Onboard the vehicle, the host processor maintained no local trajectory cache. The motor inverter controller was configured with a naive Zero-Order Hold that held the last received torque setpoint ($\tau_{\text{motor}} = 240\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$) until a new command packet arrived. Lacking an autonomous bare-metal microcontroller evaluating dynamic stopping clearance ($d_{\text{stop}}$) or enforcing hardware heartbeat watchdog timeouts, the 1.2-ton machine coasted forward at full operational velocity:

$$d_{\text{coast}} = v \cdot \Delta t_{\text{blackout}} = 1.80\text{ m/s} \times 1.420\text{ s} = 2.556\text{ m}$$

At the entrance of the vault, a structural steel building column was located at a physical clearance of $d_{\text{clearance}} = 1.200\text{ m}$. Because the vehicle traveled $2.556\text{ m}$ without initiating deceleration, it completely exhausted the available clearance buffer and overshot the impact point by:

$$\Delta d = d_{\text{coast}} - d_{\text{clearance}} = 2.556\text{ m} - 1.200\text{ m} = +1.356\text{ m}$$

The vehicle struck the solid steel column at full operational velocity ($v = 1.80\text{ m/s}$). With a total vehicle mass of $m = 1{,}200\text{ kg}$, the linear momentum carried into the collision was:

$$p = m v = 1{,}200\text{ kg} \times 1.80\text{ m/s} = 2{,}160\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s} = 2.16 \times 10^3\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$$

The kinetic energy dissipated during impact was:

$$E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 1{,}200\text{ kg} \times (1.80\text{ m/s})^2 = 1{,}944\text{ Joules}$$

The structural deceleration shock sheared the $45\text{ mm}$ alloy-steel front steering kingpin, ruptured the $210\text{ bar}$ high-pressure hydraulic steering lines, and crushed the forward $48\text{ V}$ lithium iron phosphate ($\text{LiFePO}_4$) battery modules ($42{,}000\text{ USD}$ overhaul cost). The flight-recorder telemetry ledger is detailed in @tbl-telemetry-ch10.

| Timestamp | Subsystem & Substrate | Recorded State / Telemetry Event | Physical Implication |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **$T + 84.210\text{ s}$** | 5G RF Transceiver (Vehicle) | Vehicle crosses cold-storage vault threshold; steel-clad insulation panel blocks 5G signals. | RF signal-to-noise ratio drops to $0\text{ dB}$; $100\%$ packet loss. |
| **$T + 84.250\text{ s}$** | Linux Host MPU (Vehicle) | TCP socket enters retransmit timeout; high-level VLA trajectory stream halts. | $1,420\text{ ms}$ communication blackout begins. |
| **$T + 84.500\text{ s}$** | Inverter PWM Controller | Lacking local trajectory cache or MCU watchdog, inverter latches last forward drive torque ($240\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$). | 1.2-ton machine coasts unguided at $1.8\text{ m/s}$ ($p = 2{,}160\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$). |
| **$T + 85.000\text{ s}$** | Vehicle Chassis / Front Linkage | Vehicle traverses $1.422\text{ m}$, completely exhausting physical clearance ($d_{\text{clearance}} = 1.20\text{ m}$). | Collision unavoidable; zero braking engaged. |
| **$T + 85.630\text{ s}$** | Chassis / Steel Building Pillar | Vehicle strikes steel pillar at $1.8\text{ m/s}$ ($E_k = 1{,}944\text{ J}$). | Steering kingpin shears; hydraulic lines rupture ($42{,}000\text{ USD}$ damage). |

## Engineering Contract: Hardware Placement Ledger

To establish a formal hardware mapping across compute fabrics, the systems architecture defines the **Workload Placement Specification (PLACE-01)** (@tbl-dossier-place-01).

| Subsystem Domain | Architectural Parameter | Guaranteed Invariant & Verification Boundary |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Tier 1 (MCU) Execution** | `core_type`<br>`clock_hz`<br>`sram_bytes`<br>`interrupt_jitter_us`<br>`wcet_budget_us` | ARM Cortex-M7 / Dual-Core Lockstep RISC-V<br>$480.0\text{ MHz} \pm 10\text{ ppm}$<br>$512\text{ KB}$ DTCM (Zero Heap / Static Arrays Only - `malloc=0`)<br>$\le \pm 5.0\,\mu\text{s}$ ($1000\text{ Hz}$ hard real-time timer ISR)<br>$\text{WCET} \le 175.0\,\mu\text{s}$ ($17.5\%$ CPU load margin) |
| **Tier 2 (NPU) Placement** | `model_type`<br>`target_cadence`<br>`sram_tiling_mb`<br>`arithmetic_intensity`<br>`quant_format` | Diffusion Policy / ACT Trajectory Decoders ($H=16$)<br>$20.0\text{ Hz}$ ($50.0\text{ ms}$ execution budget)<br>$\ge 8.0\text{ MB}$ dedicated on-chip weight SRAM<br>$I_{\text{arith}} \ge 120.0\text{ FLOPs/Byte}$ (SRAM resident)<br>INT8 / FP8 tensor quantization |
| **Tier 3 (MPU) Placement** | `os_kernel`<br>`max_p99_latency_ms`<br>`dram_alloc_gb`<br>`ipc_mechanism` | Linux 6.6 with `PREEMPT_RT` patch<br>$\le 35.0\text{ ms}$ nominal ($P_{99}$ scheduler jitter)<br>$4.0\text{ GB}$ LPDDR5 pinned memory (`mlockall`, zero swap)<br>Lock-free SPSC SRAM ring buffer (`alignas(64)`) |
| **Bus QoS Configuration** | `mcu_read_qos`<br>`npu_fetch_qos`<br>`dma_stream_qos`<br>`arbitration_scheme` | `QoS = 15` (Highest priority - preemption enabled for MCU reads)<br>`QoS = 10` (Medium-high priority tensor weight fetches)<br>`QoS = 4` (Throttled background camera DMA with FIFO pacing)<br>Dynamic latency-sensitive round-robin with real-time preemption |
| **Thermal Envelopes** | `t_junction_max`<br>`fan_trip_temp`<br>`dvfs_derate_temp`<br>`cooling_topology` | $85.0^\circ\text{C}$ maximum junction threshold ($T_j$)<br>$65.0^\circ\text{C}$ active cooling trigger<br>$75.0^\circ\text{C}$ proactive cadence scaling ($50\text{ Hz} \to 20\text{ Hz}$, $H=16 \to 32$)<br>IP67 sealed conduction-cooled chassis with passive heat dissipation fins |

: The Workload Placement Specification (**PLACE-01**). Quantitative silicon parameters, bus QoS priorities, and thermal boundaries bridging Architecture to Integration. {#tbl-dossier-place-01}

We audit the Workload Placement stage across the Five Physical Columns in the Co-Design Checkpoint Ledger (@tbl-placement-matrix-checkpoint).

| Physical Constraint | Placement Systems Tension | @sec-placement Architectural Resolution |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Time & Freshness** | Network and OS latency tails ($>1\text{ s}$) create blind execution. | **Strict Local Placement:** System 1 reflexes reside strictly on onboard MCU. |
| **Inertia & Stopping** | Large kinetic momentum ($p = 2{,}160\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$) requires guaranteed local stopping autonomy. | **Hardware Watchdog Timers ($15\text{ ms}$)** triggering local Category 1 braking. |
| **Actuation & Jerk** | Discrete IPC messages command jagged motor step changes. | **MCU Quintic Spline Interpolation** executed in zero-wait-state SRAM. |
| **Energy & Thermal** | Excessive DRAM accesses and NPU heating cause thermal throttling. | **On-Chip SRAM Model Tiling** and dynamic thermal derating ledgers. |
| **Silicon Determinism** | Shared UMA memory crossbar contention stalls critical threads. | **Hardware AXI QoS Priority Arbitration** (`ARQOS`/`AWQOS`). |

: Placement Co-Design Checkpoint Ledger. Systematic architectural accounting of workload placement across physical constraints. {#tbl-placement-matrix-checkpoint}


## Systems Stress-Tests: Architectural Food for Thought

Evaluating heterogeneous compute placement across physical embodiments requires confronting multi-dimensional trade-offs where statistical foundation model capacity, silicon memory bus physics, and thermal thermodynamics intersect. The following four architectural stress-tests examine critical edge cases across heterogeneous silicon placement:

#### Stress-Test 1: Cloud 70B Foundation Generalization vs. The Wireless Multipath Drop {.unnumbered}

An engineering team is deploying a fleet of $800\text{ kg}$ autonomous mobile tugs in a high-density manufacturing facility. The team must choose between:

1. **Architecture A (Offboard 70B Cloud Model):** Streams compressed stereo video over a private 5G URLLC network ($P_{50} = 4\text{ ms}$ RTT), unlocking open-world zero-shot semantic task reasoning and rich multi-modal failure recovery.
2. **Architecture B (Onboard 3B Quantized Edge Model):** Runs an INT8-quantized model locally on an embedded 30 W SoC ($T_{\text{infer}} = 350\text{ ms}$), with lower open-world generalization but zero RF dependency.

During initial testing of Architecture A, a tug traveling at $v = 2.0\text{ m/s}$ enters an aisle lined with structural steel beams and metal mesh shelving. Multipath RF reflections create a destructive interference null, triggering an unannounced $920\text{ ms}$ 5G packet blackout.

*If Architecture A is deployed, what exact mathematical lease mechanism and local microcontroller stopping envelope ($d_{\text{stop}}$) must be implemented to prevent the tug from coasting unguided into pedestrians during the $920\text{ ms}$ blackout? At what vehicle velocity and spatial clearance boundary does offboard cloud deliberation become physically unsafe regardless of wireless network QoS?*

#### Stress-Test 2: On-Chip SRAM Weight Tiling vs. LPDDR5 Memory Crossbar Saturation {.unnumbered}

A bimanual humanoid robot is designed to execute high-speed reactive manipulation ($50\text{ Hz}$ trajectory generation). The System 1.5 diffusion policy requires evaluating a 1D Temporal U-Net backbone on an embedded SoC.

The engineering team has two options:

1. **Option 1 (Large 65 MB FP16 Model on DRAM):** Generates exceptionally dexterous trajectories across 12 contact stages, but requires fetching $65\text{ MB}$ of weights from LPDDR5 DRAM per forward pass ($3.25\text{ GB/s}$ continuous DRAM traffic).
2. **Option 2 (Compact 6.5 MB INT8 Model in SRAM):** Quantized to fit entirely within the NPU's dedicated $8\text{ MB}$ on-chip static SRAM ($I_{\text{arith}} > 180\text{ FLOPs/Byte}$, zero DRAM traffic), with a $4\%$ reduction in trajectory success rate on delicate assembly tasks.

Bench testing reveals that under Option 1, the continuous DRAM weight fetches saturate the shared 128-bit memory crossbar, contending with three 4K camera DMA streams. Memory controller queues back up, inflating MCU state-read latency from $45\text{ ns}$ to $1.2\,\mu\text{s}$ and causing the 1 kHz safety enforcer to miss its timer interrupt deadline on $0.8\%$ of cycles.

*How should systems engineers structure AXI Quality-of-Service (`ARQOS`/`AWQOS`) arbitration registers and memory bus partitioning to guarantee hard real-time execution while maximizing neural model capacity? Under what operational conditions is the $4\%$ algorithmic accuracy loss of Option 2 strictly required for hardware survival?*

#### Stress-Test 3: The Sealed IP67 Conduction Chassis and the DVFS Thermal Cliff {.unnumbered}

An autonomous inspection rover operating in a chemical processing plant is housed in an IP67 hermetically sealed aluminum chassis without external cooling fans. The ambient temperature is $T_{\text{ambient}} = 45^\circ\text{C}$. The thermal resistance of the enclosure is $R_{\text{th}} = 1.80\text{ K/W}$, and the lumped thermal capacitance is $C_{\text{th}} = 25.0\text{ J/K}$ ($\tau_{\text{th}} = 45\text{ s}$).

The onboard edge SoC dissipates $P_{\text{total}} = 25.0\text{ W}$ during continuous high-cadence neural inference ($50\text{ Hz}$, $H=16$). After 98 seconds of operation, junction temperature breaches the silicon safety limit ($T_j > 85^\circ\text{C}$). The on-chip hardware power manager triggers Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS), downclocking the NPU clock from $1.2\text{ GHz}$ to $480\text{ MHz}$ ($0.40\times$). Forward inference latency explodes from $22\text{ ms}$ to $55\text{ ms}$, missing the $50\text{ ms}$ action chunking deadline and causing the vehicle to trip an emergency stop mid-mission.

*How should the system's runtime firmware implement Proactive Thermal Cadence Scaling (e.g., dynamically transitioning from $50\text{ Hz}$ to $20\text{ Hz}$ and expanding horizon from $H=16$ to $H=32$ at $T_j \ge 75^\circ\text{C}$) to achieve steady-state thermal equilibrium without sacrificing kinematic tracking accuracy?*

#### Stress-Test 4: Lock-Free SRAM IPC vs. Non-Coherent Cache Line Invalidation Overhead {.unnumbered}

A heterogeneous robotic compute architecture transfers high-rate trajectory chunks between an 8-core 64-bit ARM Cortex-A78 application processor (Linux host) and a dual-core lockstep ARM Cortex-M7 microcontroller (real-time safety executive) across a shared on-chip SRAM mailbox.

Because the Cortex-A78 operates with hierarchical L1/L2 data caches while the Cortex-M7 accesses tightly coupled DTCM SRAM without hardware cache snooping, the memory interface is non-coherent. To transfer a 2 KB trajectory chunk at $100\text{ Hz}$, the Linux driver must execute an explicit cache clean operation (`clean_dcache_range`), and the MCU must execute a cache invalidate operation (`invalidate_dcache_range`) to the Point of Coherency (PoC).

Under heavy multi-threaded Linux workloads, cache line invalidations stall the CPU pipeline and incur memory bus flush penalties that inflate average IPC handoff latency from $2.5\,\mu\text{s}$ to $180\,\mu\text{s}$, with $P_{99}$ latency spikes exceeding $850\,\mu\text{s}$.

*How must systems architects organize shared memory layouts, cache line padding (`alignas(64)`), and atomic acquire-release sequence counters to achieve microsecond-deterministic zero-copy IPC across non-coherent processor cores without risking torn reads or pipeline stalls?*


## Chapter Summary and Forward Handoff to @sec-governance

This chapter established how cognitive workloads are deliberately placed across heterogeneous silicon fabrics. Physical AI rejects the cloud illusion of fungible compute, mapping multi-rate cognitive stages across Cloud, Host MPU, Neural Accelerator NPU, and Real-Time MCU based on cadence ($0.001\text{ Hz} \to 1000\text{ Hz}$), memory bandwidth, thermal dissipation, and physical trust boundaries.

The architectural discipline of heterogeneous compute placement rests on three core pillars:

1. **Non-Fungibility of Physical Silicon:** Time-critical safety loops ($1000\text{ Hz}$) cannot be offloaded across non-deterministic wireless networks (5G/Wi-Fi) or general-purpose operating system schedulers. Generative policies propose candidate trajectories under expiring **Intent Leases** ($\tau_{\text{lease}} \le 100\text{ ms}$), while bare-metal microcontrollers maintain exclusive hardware authority over motor inverters.
2. **Deterministic Interconnects and Zero-Copy IPC:** Shared Unified Memory Architectures (UMA) require hardware **AXI QoS Priority Arbitration** (`QoS=15` for MCU, `QoS=10` for NPU, `QoS=4` for Camera DMA) to prevent video streams from starving real-time control loops. Inter-processor communication must use lock-free SRAM ring buffers with strict 64-byte cache line isolation (`alignas(64)`) to eliminate mutex context switching and cache line ping-pong.
3. **Thermodynamic Co-Design & Arithmetic Intensity:** Moving bits across off-chip DRAM consumes $750\times$ more energy per byte than on-chip arithmetic ($150\text{ pJ}$ vs $0.2\text{ pJ}$). Quantizing trajectory models to reside permanently in on-chip SRAM ($I_{\text{arith}} \ge 120\text{ FLOPs/Byte}$) eliminates DRAM bus heating. Real-time proactive thermal cadence scaling dynamically adjusts chunk horizons ($H=16 \to 32$) and inference rates ($50\text{ Hz} \to 20\text{ Hz}$) at $T_j \ge 75^\circ\text{C}$, preventing catastrophic DVFS downclocking cliffs ($>85^\circ\text{C}$).

### Advancing to @sec-governance: Runtime Governance and Safety Systems

Having established where cognitive workloads reside across heterogeneous silicon in @sec-placement, we now advance to **@sec-governance (Runtime Governance and Safety Systems: Hazard Mitigation, Dual-Heartbeat Watchdogs, and Governed Flywheels)**. 

In @sec-governance, we explore how distributed physical agents are governed during continuous operations:

- **Dual-Heartbeat Hardware Watchdogs:** Structuring bidirectional hardware and software heartbeats between Linux host MPUs and bare-metal MCUs to detect hung threads and trigger microsecond safety fallbacks.
- **Dynamic Hazard Escalation:** Implementing multi-tier fallback hierarchies (Category 2 trajectory hold $\to$ Category 1 controlled deceleration $\to$ Category 0 hardware Safe Torque Off) governed by runtime safety monitors.
- **Expiring Intent Lease Protocols:** Enforcing bounded execution leases that automatically safe the platform when semantic planners fail to refresh commands within their allocated latency budget.
- **Governed Data Flywheels:** Capturing real-world failure edge cases and out-of-distribution physical interactions for fleet-level retraining while preserving runtime determinism and operational safety.
